The preparation is the sūrah's name for the fact that the judgment is prior to the choice, and the choice is what the prior judgment receives. The fire stands, and the disbeliever arrives, and the arriving is the filling.

**The Belief That Is the Turning Point**

The condition of the verse is the double belief, the belief in Allah and the belief in His Messenger, and the doubling is the sūrah's theology in its compact form. The sūrah has stated the sending in the three offices, the witness, the deliverer of good news, the warner, and it has stated the transfer of the pledge, so that the hand given to the one sent is the hand given to the sender. The double belief is the standing form of that theology: the sender and the one sent are one faith held in two hands, and the refusal of the one is the refusal of the other. The verse states the condition in the form of the alternative, whoever does not believe, and the alternative is not named, because the alternative is everything that is not the double belief. The sūrah's frame for the choice is the frame of the one way and the many ways, and the many ways all lead to the one place the verse names.

**The Bridge Between the Two Camps**

The position of the verse in the sūrah is the reason for its brevity. It stands between the exposure of the laggards and the statement of the sovereignty, and the position is the work. The sūrah has finished with the thought of the group, and it now states the fire that stands under the thought, and after the fire it will state the ground on which the fire and the thought both stand, the kingdom of the heavens and the earth. The verse is the hinge of the movement, and the hinge is stated in one sentence because its work is to connect, not to develop. The reader passes through the verse from the census of the camp to the statement of the ground, and the passing is the sūrah's claim that the two are one movement: the camp is the ground's camp, and the ground is the camp's ground.
verses.14:
> To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth. He forgives whoever He wills, and punishes whoever He wills. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful

**Sovereignty, Not Mere Force**

The sūrah's first section spoke in the vocabulary of forces, the hosts of the heavens and the earth, and this verse speaks in the vocabulary of the kingdom, and the shift of vocabulary is the shift of subject. The hosts are what the owner has at his command, the armies and the angels and the faculties of the person, and the kingdom is what the owner owns, the heavens and the earth and everything between them. The sūrah moves from the event to the ground, and the ground is stated in the form of ownership rather than in the form of power, because the event it is grounding is not a battle but a decision, the decision to forgive or to punish. A battle is won with forces, and a decision is made by an owner, and the sūrah's second section is the section of decisions, the excuses and the refusals and the opportunities, and the decisions stand on the ownership. The verse is the foundation stone of the section, and the stone is laid before the first decision of the section is made.

**The Two Freedoms of the Owner**

The middle sentence of the verse states the two freedoms of the owner, and the two freedoms are the verse's doctrine. The first freedom is the ability: the owner can forgive all sins, and the ability is the ground of the hope that the sūrah's later verses will direct to the lagging group. The second freedom is the determination: no one may assign the categories of the forgiven and the punished, for the assignment belongs to the owner alone, and the one who assigns the categories for himself places himself beyond the owner's hand. The sūrah gives the formula its standing context elsewhere, in the address to the communities that spoke of themselves in the language of the chosen, where the Jews and the Christians each said, "We are the children of Allah and His most beloved," and the answer was the same formula, "He forgives whoever He wills and punishes whoever He wills. To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs the kingdom of the heavens and the earth" (5:18). The formula is the sūrah's answer to every presumption of the chosen, and the presumption is the one that the lagging group is about to make, when it asks to be let into a promise that was made for others.

**The Mercy That Names the Owner**

The verse ends with the two names, All-Forgiving and Most Merciful, and the ending is the sūrah's answer to the fire of the preceding verse. The fire was stated in the naked form, without its instruments and without its adjectives, and the names follow the fire, and the order is the doctrine. The sūrah does not leave the reader with the fire alone. The judgment is real, and the owner's name is real, and the names are the frame within which the judgment stands. A fire that stands outside the frame of the forgiver and the merciful is a threat, and a fire that stands inside the frame is a judgment, and the judgment is the sūrah's word for what the fire is. The names are not a softening of the fire; they are the statement of who owns the fire, and the ownership is what makes the fire a fire and not a fate. The sūrah's theology of the judgment is the theology of the owner, and the owner is named at the end of the verse in which the owner's judgment was stated.

**The Ground on Which the Opportunity Stands**

The position of the verse in the sūrah is the reason for its placement after the fire. The sūrah has exposed the laggards, stated the fire that stands under their thought, and now it lays the ground on which their atonement is possible. The exegesis fixes the point directly: the opportunity for the Bedouin who stayed behind to make amends is presented in the sixteenth verse, and the opportunity stands on this verse, for the atonement is an act of the owner's freedom, and the owner forgives whom He wills. The sūrah states the ground before it states the opportunity, so that the opportunity is read on the ground, and the reading is the sūrah's claim. The group that stayed behind is not beyond the reach of the forgiveness, because the forgiveness belongs to the owner of the kingdom, and the owner's hand is over the group and over the promise and over the fire. The verse is the sūrah's way of keeping the door open while stating the door's frame.

**The Formula's Standing Form**

The formula of the verse is a standing form in the Quran, and the sūrah's use of it here fixes the form as the ground of the second section. The formula appears in the sūrah of the cow, where the ownership of everything in the heavens and on the earth is stated together with the two freedoms, "To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth... He forgives whoever He wills, and punishes whoever He wills. And Allah is Most Capable of everything" (2:284), and it appears in the sūrah of the family and in the sūrah of the covenant and in the sūrah of the stars, and the range of the appearances fixes the formula as the standing ground of the Quran's own address. The sūrah's second section, from the excuses of the laggards to the approval of the pledge, stands on the formula, and each verse of the section is a decision made on the ground the verse lays. The formula is the sūrah's foundation, and the foundation is stated once, at the head of the section, so that the section's decisions are read as standing on it.
verses.15:
> Those who stayed behind will say, when you ˹believers˺ set out to take the spoils of war, “Let us accompany you.” They wish to change Allah’s promise. Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “You will not accompany us. This is what Allah has said before.” They will then say, “In fact, you are driven by jealousy against us!” The truth is: they can hardly comprehend

**The Refusal That Returns**

The group of the previous verses now appears in its second movement, and the movement is the return. When the believers set out for the spoils, the spoils that the sūrah's own earlier verses had promised, the group that stayed behind for the pilgrimage says, let us follow you. The sūrah records the return in the group's own words, and the recording is the portrait. The group is shown in its two movements, the refusal and the return, and the two movements together are the state. A group that refuses the pilgrimage and returns for the spoils is a group whose relation to the event is the relation of the calculator, and the calculator's movement is the sūrah's diagnosis of the group. The verse does not need to state the diagnosis in terms of the heart, because the two movements state it in terms of the fact, and the fact is the sūrah's evidence. The refusal was the calculation, and the return is the calculation's proof.

**The Promise They Wish to Change**

The sūrah's charge against the return is the sentence that names the object of the wish: they wish to change the promise of Allah. The exegesis fixes the promise. The victory of Khaybar, the campaign that followed Ḥudaibiyah, was understood to have been promised to those who had been present at the pledge, in exchange for the pilgrimage they had been unable to complete. The promise was the reward of the pledge, and the reward of the pledge belongs to the pledgers, and the group's wish is to insert itself into the promise, to change its terms, to take a share of what the pledge bought. The charge is therefore not the wish to go but the wish to change, and the changing is the sin. A promise that can be changed by the request of the one who missed it is not a promise but an offer, and the sūrah's statement of the charge is its refusal of the offer. The promise stands, and the request is the attempt to move the promise, and the attempt is what the verse condemns.

**The Rejection and Its Ground**

The answer the sūrah commands is the rejection, and the rejection is stated in a form that fixes its ground. You will not follow us, and the ground is stated in the same breath: this is what Allah has said before. The rejection is not the preference of the companions, and it is not the decision of the Prophet acting on his own judgment; it is the enforcement of a prior statement, the promise that was made before the return was asked. The sūrah's form is the command to say followed by the statement of the prior, and the form is the doctrine. A rejection that rests on a prior word is not a refusal but a confirmation, and the confirmation is the sūrah's way of saying that the promise was never negotiable. The group asked to change the promise, and the answer is that the promise was already stated, and the stating is what the group's wish is against. The prior word stands, and the return falls against it.

**The Counter-Accusation and Its Non-Answer**

The group's response to the rejection is the counter-accusation, and the sūrah records it without engaging it. In fact, you are driven by jealousy against us, the group says, and the saying is the form the refusal takes when the ground has been removed. The group's wish has been met with the prior word, and the prior word is not an argument the group can meet, because the prior word is the promise itself. A person whose excuse has been removed does not accept the removal; he attributes the removal to a motive in the other, and the motive he names is jealousy, the one motive that would make the rejection a wrong. The sūrah's non-engagement is its answer. The counter-accusation is not disproved, because the disproof is not the point; the point is that the counter-accusation is the sign of the ground's removal, and the sign is what the sūrah records. The group that has lost the argument moves the argument to the character of the other, and the moving is the group's final position.

**The Little That Is Understood**

The verse's final word is the state of understanding, and the state is the sūrah's name for the group's relation to the promise. The truth is: they can hardly comprehend. The exegesis gives the sense in two lines. On the one line, the little comprehension is the comprehension of the worldly, the group understands the affairs of the world, the spoils and the easy victory, and it does not understand the affair of the promise, which is not a worldly affair. On the other line, the comprehension is little in the matter of the religion, and the little is the state. And some render the word as a few, so that only a few of the group understand, and the few are the exception that proves the state. The sūrah's claim, in either reading, is that the group's calculation is a worldly calculation, and the worldly calculation does not reach the promise, because the promise is not of the order of the worldly. The incomprehension is not a defect of the mind; it is the relation of the mind to an object that is not of its order, and the verse's final word is the sūrah's way of stating the relation.
verses.16:
> Say to nomadic Arabs, who stayed behind, “You will be called ˹to fight˺ against a people of great might, who you will fight unless they submit. If you then obey, Allah will grant you a fine reward. But if you turn away as you did before, He will inflict upon you a painful punishment.”

**The Address Turned to the Future**

The sūrah now turns its address to the group as a prophecy, and the prophecy is the summons. You will be called against a people of great might, the verse says, and the calling is not yet issued. The verse states the future in the present, so that the future is prepared, and the preparation is the sūrah's way of fixing the group's present choice on the ground of its future calling. The group has been dealt with in the sūrah as a present, the excuse and the refusal and the return and the counter-accusation, and the verse now deals with it as a future, the coming call and the coming fight. The two tenses together are the sūrah's portrait of the group: a group that is addressed in the present and prepared for the future, and the preparation is the sūrah's claim that the group's story is not over, and the not-over is what the calling preserves.

**The People of Great Might**

The exegesis divides on the identity of the people of great might, and the three lines of the division are worth weighing. One line takes them as the tribe of the Ḥanīfa, the community that the armies of the first caliph, Abū Bakr, defeated in the years after the Prophet's death. Another takes the verse as pointing ahead to the future wars against the two great empires, Byzantium and Persia, the powers that would come against the Muslim state. A third takes them as the tribes of the Hawāzin and the Thaqīf, the confederacy that met the Muslim army in the field after the conquest of Makkah. The third line is the one the later history first confirms, and the confirmation is the battle of Ḥunayn, the first great fight the community engaged in after the treaty, fought by the very community that had pledged at Ḥudaibiyah against a people of great might, the Hawāzin with their allies. The sūrah's description, the people of great might, is the description of that fight, and the fight is the calling's first arrival. The verse's future was the sūrah's way of saying that the community that had been turned back from the Sacred Mosque would go on to meet the might of Arabia in the field.

**The Two Options Stated as One**

The verse states the options of the calling in a single clause, and the single clause is the sūrah's point. You will fight them, or they will submit, and the sense, the exegesis gives, is the two options the idolatrous tribes of Arabia were given when the Muslim army confronted them. The clause joins the two options with the or, and the joining is the removal of the third option, the option of staying behind and waiting. The group's pattern, the pattern of staying behind for the pilgrimage and returning for the spoils, is removed from the menu by the clause, and the removal is the sūrah's claim. The calling will not wait for the group, and the group's waiting is no longer a position the sūrah recognizes. The two options stand, and the standing is the sūrah's way of saying that the future of the group is the future of the fight, and the fight is what the calling is for.

**The Reward and the Punishment in Their Balance**

The verse states the two outcomes of the calling in their balance, and the balance is the sūrah's way of keeping the choice open. If the group then obeys, the obedience is met with a fine reward, and the exegesis gives the reward in its two parts: the spoils and the aid of the fight in this life, and the Garden in the next. If the group turns away, the turning away is met with a painful punishment, and the reference of the turning away is stated in the verse's own terms: as you turned away before, the refusal of the pilgrimage. The balance is the sūrah's doctrine. The future obedience is matched to the reward, and the future turning away is matched to the punishment, and the matching is what makes the calling a choice rather than a command. The group is not ordered to obey; it is shown the two outcomes, and the showing is the sūrah's way of leaving the choice with the one who makes it.

**The Opportunity That the Ground Made Possible**

The exegesis fixes the function of the verse in the sūrah's treatment of the lagging group, and the function is the opportunity. The ground was laid in the fourteenth verse, the sovereignty of the owner and the two freedoms of the owner, and the opportunity is the sixteenth, the calling that is offered to the group. The calling is the means of the atonement, for the obedience of the fight is the obedience that cancels the refusal, and the cancellation is the sūrah's way of completing its treatment of the group. The three verses form the treatment: the ground, the promise that the ground carries, and the opportunity that the promise preserves. The group that stayed behind is not closed off from the sūrah's address; it is addressed in the three forms, and the three forms are the sūrah's statement of the group's position, a position that is judged and grounded and offered, in that order, and the order is the sūrah's claim.
verses.17:
> There is no blame on the blind, or the disabled, or the sick ˹for staying behind˺. And whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger will be admitted by Him into Gardens under which rivers flow. But whoever turns away will be subjected by Him to a painful punishment

**The Exemption of Those Who Cannot**

The sūrah moves from the group to the individual, and the movement is the correction. The lagging group was dealt with as a group, the excuse and the refusal and the return, and the verse now divides the stayers into their individuals, and the division is the sūrah's correction of the group's portrait. Not everyone who stayed behind has refused, the verse says; some cannot go, and the cannot is the ground of the exemption. The list the verse gives is three: the blind, the disabled, the sick, and the three are the three faculties that the journey requires. Sight for the road, movement for the way, health for the burden. A person who lacks one of the three lacks the ground of the going, and the lack is what the verse exempts. The exemption is the sūrah's way of saying that the stayers are not one group but several, and the several are to be divided before they are judged. The judgment of the group in the earlier verses was the judgment of the group's state, and the state of the individual is the state the verse now addresses.

**The Parallel Verse and Its Frame**

The Quran gives the exemption in its full form elsewhere, in the sūrah that closes the revelation, where the parallel is stated with its condition and its fourth category: "There is no blame on the weak, the sick, or those lacking the means ˹if they stay behind˺, as long as they are true to Allah and His Messenger. There is no blame on the good-doers. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful" (9:91). The parallel adds to the sūrah's list the fourth category, those lacking the means, the poverty that is the ground of the stay as the blindness is the ground of it, and it adds the condition, the truth to Allah and His Messenger, which fixes the exemption on the heart rather than on the body alone. The two verses together state the doctrine of the exemption in its full form. The sūrah's verse gives the exemption in its bare form, the three categories and the no blame, and the parallel gives it in its full form, the four categories and the condition. The bare form is the sūrah's way of stating the principle, and the full form is the Quran's way of stating the application, and the application is the principle in its details.

**The Obedience That Admits**

The verse's second sentence states the pair in its plainest form, and the plainness is the sūrah's move. Whoever obeys Allah and His Messenger, the one who has the ground of the going and takes it, is admitted by Him into the Gardens under which rivers flow, and the admission is the Gardens. The sūrah states the obedience as the condition of the admission, and the condition is the double obedience, the obedience to Allah and the obedience to His Messenger, the same double that the belief of the thirteenth verse stated in its positive form. The Quran states the stark contrast of the obedience and the turning away throughout its text, and the sūrah of the light gives it in the form the sūrah's verse takes: the obedience to God and to the Messenger is the obedience that carries the person to the right guidance, and the messenger is accountable only for the burden with which he was charged, while each of the people is accountable for the burden with which they were charged (24:54). The sūrah's verse takes the contrast and states it without the intermediate, the obedience admits, and the turning away punishes, and the without-the-intermediate is the sūrah's way of stating the freedom of the person who has the ground.

**The Turning-Away That Punishes**

The verse's third sentence completes the pair, and the completion is the statement of the freedom. Whoever turns away, the one who has the ground of the going and refuses it, is subjected by Him to a painful punishment, and the punishment is the pair's other half. The sūrah's form is the one subject carrying the two alternatives, the same whoever in the two sentences, and the one subject is the sūrah's way of stating that the two alternatives are the two positions of the one person. The person who can go and does not go is in the position of the turning away, and the person who cannot go is in the position of the exemption, and the two positions are the sūrah's division of the stayers. The painful punishment is the word the sūrah has used for the punishment of the group that turned away in the sixteenth verse, and the reuse of the word fixes the relation: the turning away of the individual is the turning away of the group, and the group's turning away is the individual's. The sūrah's treatment of the stayers is complete when the three forms are stated, the exemption, the opportunity, and the exposure, and the verse is the one that states the first of the three in its plainest form.

**The Verse That Divides the Stayers**

The position of the verse in the sūrah's treatment of the lagging group is the reason for its function. The sūrah has exposed the group's state in the two verses that followed the first section, it has stated the group's return and its wish to change the promise, it has offered the group the calling as the opportunity of the atonement, and now it divides the stayers into their individuals. The division is the sūrah's final word on the group, and the final word is the division into three: those who cannot, those who can and will, and those who can and refuse. The three have three fates, the exemption, the admission, the punishment, and the three fates are the sūrah's census of the camp's interior. The group that stayed behind is not one group in the sūrah's account; it is three groups, and the three are the sūrah's statement of the fact that the state of the group is the state of the individuals, and the individuals are to be divided before they are judged. The verse is the sūrah's way of completing the census, and the census is the sūrah's claim that the judgment is the judgment of the person, not of the population.
verses.18:
> Indeed, Allah was pleased with the believers when they pledged allegiance to you ˹O Prophet˺ under the tree. He knew what was in their hearts, so He sent down serenity upon them and rewarded them with a victory at hand

**The Pleasure That Is the First Reward**

The verse opens with the pleasure, and the pleasure is the first of the rewards the verse assigns to the pledgers, and the first reward is the one that is not a thing but a relation. Allah was pleased with the believers, the verse states, and the stating is the sūrah's hierarchy of the rewards. The pleasure comes before the serenity, and the serenity comes before the victory, and the order is the sūrah's claim about the order of the good: the relation precedes the calm, and the calm precedes the event. A reward that is a relation is not added to the person; it is the person's standing, and the standing is what the sūrah's remaining verses will show to be the ground of the rest. The community's own memory took the pleasure as the point of the event, and the name it gave the pledge, the pledge of good pleasure, is this verse's word made into a title. The sūrah's opening of the verse with the pleasure is its way of saying that the event at the tree was, first of all, a matter of the relation between the community and its Lord, and the rest of the event is the relation's consequences.

**The Tree and the Number**

The sūrah does not name the tree, and the tradition that preserves the event names it. The tree under which the pledge was made was a samurah, an acacia, the tafsīr tradition reports, and the naming is the community's way of making the verse concrete. The number of the pledgers is reported in two figures, the one over thirteen hundred, the other about fifteen hundred, and the two figures are the range of the community's own count. The form of the pledge is reported in two readings, and the two readings are the range of the community's own memory: the majority of the accounts take the pledge as the pledge that they would not flee, and some take it as the pledge that they would fight the Quraysh until death, and the two readings are not opposed, because a pledge that is not to flee is, in the situation, the pledge to fight. The sūrah's silence on the details and the tradition's naming of them are the two layers of the event, and the two layers together are the sūrah's account. The verse states the pledge in its bare form, under the tree, and the bare form is what the details serve, and the serving is the tradition's way of keeping the verse's bare form full.

**What Was in Their Hearts**

The sūrah states what the Lord knew of the pledgers, and the stating is the verse's turn to the interior. He knew what was in their hearts, and the exegesis gives the knowledge in its two readings, and the two readings are the two states the hearts could hold. On the one reading, the hearts held the sincerity and the loyalty with which the pledge was taken, and the knowledge is the knowledge of the positive state. On the other reading, the hearts held the dejection they felt at not being able to complete the pilgrimage, and the knowledge is the knowledge of the negative state, and the serenity that follows is the consolation of the dejection. The two readings are not opposed, because the hearts held both at once, the sincerity of the pledge and the dejection of the turn-back, and the knowledge is the knowledge of the whole. The sūrah's point is that the pledge was a matter of the heart, and the hand under the tree was the body of the heart's state, and the heart's state is what the verse states as known before it states it as rewarded. The pledgers are known, and the knowing is the ground of the pleasure and the serenity and the victory.

**The Serenity's Second Descent**

The verse is the sūrah's second sending of the serenity, and the sending follows the first at the point of the second strain. The first was at the turning back from the Sacred Mosque, and the second is at the tree, when the envoy was believed killed and the community had bound itself to a fight it had not come to make. The context of the second descent is the week's accumulation, the dejection of the turn-back, the anxiety of the delay, the terms of the treaty that some of the faithful resented, and the serenity is the sūrah's way of stating that the community's state at the tree was the state of being held. The holding is the sūrah's description of the event from the inside, and the inside is what the sūrah's first section had described from the outside, the serenity sent down so that the faith should increase. The second descent is the first in its consequence, and the consequence is the state of the pledgers, a community that has made its pledge in the state of being held, and the holding is what makes the pledge the pledge the sūrah rewards.

**The Victory That Is Near**

The verse's final word is the victory, and the victory is stated in the form of the nearness, a victory at hand. The exegesis fixes the reference in its two lines, and the lines are the two events the nearness could name. The more likely, on the sūrah's own account, is the conquest of Khaybar, which followed Ḥudaibiyah soon after the departure, and the tafsīr tradition states the reference in those terms, the near victory being the conquest of Khaybar following their departure from Ḥudaibiyah. The other line takes the near victory as the conquest of Makkah, the event that the sūrah's later verse about the fulfilled vision will promise in its full form. The two readings are the two stages of the nearness, the near that arrives first and the near that arrives last, and the sūrah's word, at hand, holds both. The victory is not yet, and the not-yet is the nearness, and the verse's reward is a future that is already promised, and the future is the sūrah's way of saying that the event at the tree was the beginning, not the end, and the beginning is what the sūrah's next verse will complete.
verses.19:
> and many spoils of war they will gain. For Allah is Almighty, All-Wise

**A Reward Stated in Two Halves**

The verse is the second half of a sentence that began in the previous verse, and the first half named the victory at hand, while this one names the spoils that follow the victory. The reward of the pledge, in the sūrah's account, is a pair, the event and the substance, the victory and the spoils, and the pair is stated across the two verses so that each half carries the other. The sūrah's structure here is its way of saying that the reward is not one thing but two, and that the two are the sūrah's statement of what the pledge bought. The victory was the near event, the spoils are the gain that the event carries, and the carrying is the sūrah's way of fixing the relation between the two. A victory without spoils is a name, and spoils without a victory are a number, and the sūrah's pair is what makes the reward the reward it states. The sūrah's pair also holds the two orders of the community's memory together: the victory came first in the memory of the event, and the spoils came first in the history that followed it, and the two orders are what the sūrah keeps in one sentence.

**The Spoils of the Near Campaign**

The exegesis fixes the spoils in their first reference, and the first reference is the campaign that followed the treaty. The abundant spoils, on the sūrah's own account, are the spoils of Khaybar, the fortified oasis to the north of Madinah, and the campaign for it was the first campaign the community engaged in after the departure from Ḥudaibiyah. The spoils promised to the pledgers at the tree were paid at Khaybar, and the payment is the sūrah's way of making the promise history. The exegesis notes the sequence of the events: the departure from the valley, the return to Medina, and then the march for the oasis, and the sequence is the sūrah's way of saying that the payment followed the promise without a gap. The verse states the spoils in the future tense, they will gain, and the future tense becomes the past at Khaybar, and the becoming is the sūrah's claim. The promise was stated in the valley outside Mecca, and the promise was paid in the oasis to the north of Madinah, and the distance between the two is the sūrah's way of saying that the reward of the pledge was not a local thing.

**The Spoils Beyond the Near Campaign**

The exegesis preserves a second line of reference, and the second line takes the spoils as the spoils of the conquests that followed the Prophet's life, the conquests against the two great empires, Persia and Byzantium. The two lines are not opposed, because the word the sūrah uses is a plural that holds both, the spoils of the near campaign and the spoils of the far conquest, and the plural is the sūrah's way of saying that the promise is not limited to a single event. The sūrah's statement of the spoils is the statement of a line, and the line is what the sūrah's later verses will show to be the history of the community. The promise of the verse is the line, and the line is the sūrah's way of saying that the reward of the pledge extends beyond the horizon of the event that produced it.

**The Pledge and Its Pay**

The sūrah's account of the event itself, preserved in the exegesis, gives the verse its setting. The pilgrims waited at the valley for the answer of the people of Mecca, and the envoy carried the statement of the peaceful intention into the city, and while the negotiation ran its course, the rumor of the envoy's death reached the camp, and the rumor was the occasion of the summons. All who were present, with the single exception of one hypocrite, passed to the one who sat beneath the acacia and put their hands in his, and the passing is the event the verse rewards. The community's own memory took the event as the point of the sūrah's first verse, and the report preserved in the tafsīr tradition states the judgment in the community's own terms: the conquest of Makkah, the report says, was indeed a victory, but the victory that the companions named was the pledge of good pleasure, made on the day of Ḥudaibiyah. And it is reported of the Prophet that he spoke of the pledgers in words that kept the tree in the community's memory: those who pledged beneath it would not enter the Fire, and the saying is the sūrah's way of stating the pay of the pledge, the pay that the verse's spoils are the first installment of. The acacia, the tree, the hand of the one sent, the pledge taken in the heat of the rumor: the elements of the account that the verse leaves bare are filled in by the tradition, and the filling is the community's way of keeping the event alive.

**The Two Names That Close the Verse**

The verse closes with the two names, Almighty and All-Wise, and the closing is the sūrah's way of grounding the reward. The names are the sūrah's standing form for the close of a statement, and the form here is the statement of the ground on which the spoils stand. The Almighty is the name of the one who holds the spoils in his power, and the All-Wise is the name of the one who chooses what he gives and when he gives it, and the two names together are the sūrah's way of saying that the promise of the verse is not a hope but an arrangement. The sūrah's second half closes its statement of the reward with the names, and the names are the sūrah's way of saying that the reward is held by the one who is capable of it and wise in its giving.
verses.20:
> Allah has promised you ˹believers˺ abundant spoils, which you will gain, so He hastened this ˹truce˺ for you. And He has held people’s hands back from ˹harming˺ you, so it may be a sign for the believers, and so He may guide you along the Straight Path

**The Promise Stated Twice**

The spoils are promised again, and the second promise is the sūrah's way of saying that the spoils are the center of its second half. The previous verse stated the spoils as the second half of the reward of the pledge, and this verse states them as a promise in their own right, a promise made to the believers as a community. The exegesis gives the relation of the two mentions in its two lines: the second is a reiteration of the first for the purpose of emphasis, or it is a reference to greater spoils beyond those named in the previous verse. The two lines are the sūrah's way of saying that the repetition is not a redundancy, and that the center of the sūrah's second half is the statement of the reward. The three verses of the reward, from the spoils they will gain to the gains beyond the reach, form the sūrah's census of the promise, and the census is the sūrah's claim about the treaty.

**The Hastening of the Truce**

The middle clause of the verse is the one that carries the sūrah's paradox, and the paradox is the hastening. He hastened this for you, the verse states, and the this, on the exegesis's account, is the truce, the advantage the Muslims gained through the treaty of Ḥudaibiyah. The exegesis gives the hastening in its three readings: the hastening is the advantage of the treaty itself, the spoils arrived through the peace that the treaty made; the hastening is the conquest of Khaybar, the near campaign that the treaty opened; and the hastening is the attainment of the spoils in general, the spoils that the delay of the pilgrimage seemed to postpone. The three readings hold the paradox at once. The delay was the hastening, and the turning back was the arrival, and the sūrah's word for the event is the word for the quickening. The community that was turned back from the Sacred Mosque was hastened toward the spoils, and the hastening is the sūrah's way of saying that the week at Ḥudaibiyah was not a loss of time but a gain of it.

**The Hands Held Back as a Sign**

The verse states the holding back of the people's hands in the form of a sign, and the form is the sūrah's doctrine. The holding back is what may be a sign for the believers, and a sign is something that is made in order to be read, and the sign here is the absence, the hands that were raised and did not strike. The sūrah's doctrine of the sign is the doctrine of the non-event, and the non-event is what the believers are commanded to read. The event that did not happen at Ḥudaibiyah, the battle that did not come, is the sign, and the sign is the sūrah's way of saying that the community is to learn from the absence as it learns from the presence. The reading of the sign is the guidance that the verse states, and the guidance is the sūrah's name for the state of the community that has read the event. The sign is made for the reading, and the reading is the guidance, and the guidance is the sūrah's way of closing the account of the spoils with the state of the community that receives them.

**The Guidance That the Sign Carries**

The verse's final purpose is the guidance along the Straight Path, and the purpose is the sūrah's way of saying that the event at Ḥudaibiyah is a lesson. The lesson is the holding back, and the holding back is the lesson because it is the thing the community did not expect, the hands that were raised and did not strike, the battle that was probable and did not come. A community that reads the holding back as a sign is a community that is guided, and the guidance is the sūrah's name for the state of the community that has learned from the event. The sūrah's statement of the guidance is its way of saying that the spoils are not the end of the account, and that the end is the state of the community that receives them. The community that receives the spoils in the state of guidance is the community the sūrah describes, and the description is the sūrah's claim about the event and its consequence.

**The Inner Wealth of the Path**

The exegesis preserves a spiritual reading of the verse, and the reading is the sūrah's way of extending the spoils beyond the field. The abundant spoils, on this reading, are the inner riches received by those who follow the spiritual path, and the hastening is the hastening of the inner arrival. The reading is the sūrah's way of saying that the spoils are of two kinds, the spoils of the field and the spoils of the heart, and that the two kinds are the sūrah's statement of the reward in its full range. The community that receives the spoils of the field is the community that is trained to receive the spoils of the heart, and the training is the sūrah's way of saying that the reward of the pledge is not a single kind of good. The two kinds stand in the verse together, and the standing is the sūrah's claim about the reward and its recipients.
verses.21:
> And ˹there are˺ other gains which are beyond your reach that Allah is keeping in store ˹for you˺. For Allah is Most Capable of everything

**The Gains Beyond the Reach**

The verse is the third statement of the reward, and the third statement is the sūrah's way of extending the promise beyond the horizon of the event. Other gains, the verse says, and the other is the word that carries the extension. The gains are other than the spoils named in the two previous verses, and they are beyond the reach of the community at the moment the verse is stated. The exegesis gives the reference in its lines: further spoils of war beyond the spoils of the near campaign, the gains of the oasis to the north, the conquest of the city of the house, the future wars against the two empires of Persia and Byzantium, the whole range of the openings that would come to the Muslim community, or the rewards of the inner order. The plural holds them all, and the sūrah's word for them, beyond your reach, is the sūrah's way of saying that the promise extends beyond what the community can see. The gains are kept in store, and the keeping in store is the sūrah's name for the state of the promise before its arrival.

**The North That the Treaty Opened**

The exegesis gives the strategic point of the verse, and the point is the geography of the promise. The army of the community could not, before the truce, march on the northern frontier, and the reason was the exposure of the south. A force that moved north with the power of Mecca behind it was a force whose rear was open, and the open rear was the ground of the holding. The truce closed that exposure, and the closing is what the sūrah's verse states in its words of the gains beyond the reach. The march for the oasis became possible, and the possible was the promise made concrete. The treaty is therefore the sūrah's turning point in the politics of the community: it closed the southern front and opened the northern one, and the closing and the opening are the sūrah's way of saying that the peace was the precondition of the war that followed. The gains beyond the reach were the gains of the north, and the north was opened by the peace, and the opening is the sūrah's claim about the event.

**The Breaking and Its Consequence**

The exegesis completes the strategic picture with the breaking of the treaty, and the breaking is the second movement of the sūrah's claim. The people of Mecca, when they broke the truce, did so by backing an allied tribe in a raid on a tribe that stood with the Muslims, and the backing released the Muslims from the terms, and the release was the freedom to turn the whole force of the community upon the south. The focus upon the south was the campaign that ended in the conquest of Makkah, and the conquest was the arrival of the gains that the first verse of the sūrah had announced. The treaty, in the sūrah's account, is the hinge of the community's political fortune: it produced the spoils of the north, and its breaking produced the conquest of the south, and the two together are the sūrah's way of saying that the treaty was the precondition of both. The hinge is the sūrah's name for the event, and the name is the sūrah's claim about the treaty's place in the history it opened.

**The Capability That Holds the Promise**

The verse closes with the name of capability, and the closing is the sūrah's way of grounding the promise in its third form. Allah is Most Capable of everything, and the capability is the ground of the gains that are beyond the community's reach. The community cannot reach the gains, the sūrah says, and the one who promises them is the one who is capable of them, and the capability is the sūrah's way of saying that the promise is not a hope but an arrangement. A hope depends on the one who hopes, and an arrangement depends on the one who arranges, and the sūrah's closing of the verse with the capability is its way of placing the promise on the ground of the arranger. A promise that rests on the capability of its promiser is not an expression of the promiser's wish, and the sūrah's refusal of the wish is its way of fixing the promise as an act of power. The sūrah's second half closes its statement of the reward with the capability, and the capability is the sūrah's way of saying that the reward of the treaty is held by the one who is capable of everything that the reward requires, from the opening of the northern march to the arrival of the conquests the community had not yet seen.

**Three Points of the Promise**

The three verses of the reward form the sūrah's census of the promise, and the census is the sūrah's way of saying that the promise is not one event but a process. The spoils they will gain is the first point of the census, the spoils promised and hastened is the second, and the gains beyond the reach is the third, and the three points together are the sūrah's statement of the reward in its full range. The census is the sūrah's way of saying that the treaty was the beginning of a line, and that the line is the sūrah's claim about the event. The process that the census states is the process of the community's history, and the history is the sūrah's way of making the promise the account, and the account the promise.
verses.22:
> If the disbelievers were to fight you, they would certainly flee. Then they would never find any protector or helper

**The Counterfactual Stated**

The sūrah now states what would have happened had the treaty not been made, and the stating is the sūrah's way of answering the question the event raised. If the disbelievers were to fight you, the verse says, and the if is the counterfactual, the battle that did not come. The exegesis gives the sense: had the disbelievers of Mecca chosen to attack rather than to make a treaty, they would have been destroyed and would have fled from battle. The counterfactual is the sūrah's way of saying that the treaty was not the result of the Muslims' weakness, and that the turning back was not the result of the Quraysh's strength. The question the event raised was the one the companions themselves raised, the question of how a triumph could be spoken of when the camp had been turned back, and the sūrah's answer to the question is the counterfactual, the battle that would have come and would have ended in the flight. The sūrah's statement of the counterfactual is its answer to the objection that the first verse's triumph was a triumph of words, and the answer is that the words rest on the force that the counterfactual names.

**The Flight and the Absence of the Helper**

The verse states the two outcomes of the counterfactual in their order, the flight and the absence of the helper, and the order is the sūrah's way of stating the end of the one who fights and loses. They would have turned their backs, and then they would have found neither protector nor helper, and the then is the sūrah's way of fixing the sequence. The exegesis gives the range of the absence: it refers to the situation in this life and in the next, and the Quran states the formula elsewhere in its standing form, in the sūrah of the women, where the proud and the arrogant are the ones who find no helper, "And besides Allah they will find no protector or helper" (4:173). The sūrah's verse takes the standing formula and applies it to the counterfactual, and the application is the sūrah's way of saying that the end of the hostile is the end the Quran has already named. The absence of the helper is the sūrah's name for the state of the one whose power has gone, and the state is what the counterfactual reaches.

**The Standing That Made the Choice**

The exegesis gives the point that explains the Quraysh's choice, and the point is the standing of the Quraysh in Arabia. The power, wealth, and prestige of the Quraysh were derived from their being the keepers of the Kaʿbah, and the keeping was the source of their standing with all the tribes of the peninsula. An attack on a large group of pilgrims, unarmed and in the state of visit, would have compromised that standing irreparably, and the compromise was the cost the Quraysh would have paid for the battle. The counterfactual is therefore the sūrah's way of saying that the Quraysh's own standing was the reason they chose the treaty. The attack would have cost them the very thing that was their power, and the cost is what the sūrah's statement of the flight names. The Quraysh did not choose the treaty out of weakness, the sūrah implies; they chose it out of the arithmetic of their standing, and the arithmetic is the sūrah's way of saying that the peace was the stronger position.

**The Peace as the Stronger Position**

The counterfactual is the sūrah's way of stating the strength of the peace, and the strength is the sūrah's claim about the event. The community that was turned back from the Sacred Mosque was not the weaker party in the valley, and the turning back was not the result of the Quraysh's superiority. The sūrah's statement of the counterfactual is its way of saying that the treaty was the result of the Quraysh's calculation, and the calculation was made on the ground of the standing and the cost. The peace was the position from which the Quraysh could not fight without paying the price of their own standing, and the price is what the sūrah's counterfactual states. The sūrah's claim, by the verse, is that the triumph announced in the first verse was a triumph of the position, and the position was the peace, and the peace was the result of the arithmetic that the verse states. The claim does not soften the event, and the counterfactual is not a comfort given to a community that had suffered. It is a statement of the position, and the position is what the first verse's triumph rests on, and the resting is the sūrah's way of saying that the words of the first verse were spoken from the ground the counterfactual names.

**Closing the Spoils Account**

The position of the verse is the reason for its function. The three verses of the reward have stated the spoils, the hastening, and the gains beyond the reach, and the sūrah now states the counterfactual, and the counterfactual is the sūrah's way of closing the account of the spoils. The spoils were not the result of a military advantage that the community held, the sūrah says, and they were not the result of a weakness that the community suffered. They were the result of the treaty, and the treaty was the result of the Quraysh's calculation, and the calculation is the sūrah's way of saying that the reward of the treaty is the reward of the peace. The sūrah's second half is about to turn to the wont of God and the holding back of the hands, and the counterfactual is the bridge between the two, the bridge that carries the reader from the account of the spoils to the statement of the pattern.
verses.23:
> ˹This is˺ Allah’s way, already long established ˹in the past˺. And you will find no change in Allah’s way

**A Standing Pattern, Named**

The verse names the pattern, and the name is the word for the wont, the way, the standing form of the dealings of God with the communities he addresses. The sūrah states the event of Ḥudaibiyah as an instance of the wont, and the stating is the sūrah's way of saying that the event is not an exception. The exegesis fixes the reference in its usual line: the wont here is the way God deals with those who fight his prophets, and the Quran states the wont in its plainest form in the sūrah of the divorce, where the declaration is that God and his messengers will surely prevail. The sūrah's verse takes the wont and applies it to the event, and the application is the sūrah's claim. The event at Ḥudaibiyah, the turning back and the treaty and the held-back hands, is the wont made visible in the community's own history, and the visibility is what the sūrah's naming gives it.

**The Pattern Stated in the Past**

The verse states the wont in the past, and the past is the sūrah's way of saying that the pattern is not a new thing. The way of Allah, already long established, the verse says, and the establishment is in the communities that came before. The Quran states the wont in its earlier addresses, in the sūrah of the fleet, where the formula of the no-change is given in its standing form: "You will find no change in the way of Allah, nor will you find it diverted" (35:43). The sūrah's verse takes the formula and states it in the form of the event, and the form is the sūrah's way of saying that the event is the wont made present. The past and the present stand together in the verse, and the standing is the sūrah's claim: the community that stands in the valley outside Mecca stands in the line of the communities that stood before it, and the line is the wont. The line is the sūrah's way of placing the community of the valley in the standing order of the addressed, and the order is the sūrah's claim about the community's place in the history of the address, a history that the sūrah's own earlier verses have traced from the first community to the last.

**The No-Change Stated**

The verse's second sentence is the formula of the no-change, and the formula is the sūrah's way of closing the statement of the pattern. You will find no change in Allah's way, and the finding is the sūrah's way of stating that the pattern is not subject to the events that seem to alter it. The exegesis preserves a grammatical note on the verse, and the note is the sūrah's way of saying that the formula is a standing one. The rendering of the verse in the reading tradition is the nominative, an accepted interpretation, and the recitation is the accusative, in which case the word is the object of an implied verb. The note is a detail, and the detail is the sūrah's way of fixing the formula in the standing tradition of the reading. The formula stands, and the standing is what the sūrah's event illustrates, and the illustration is the sūrah's claim about the relation of the event to the pattern.

**The Reading the Community Is Taught**

The wont is the sūrah's way of teaching the community to read its own history, and the teaching is the sūrah's doctrine. A community that reads its events as exceptions is a community that is not reading the sūrah, and a community that reads them as instances of the pattern is a community that is reading it. The sūrah's statement of the wont is its way of saying that the event at Ḥudaibiyah is an instance, and that the instance is to be read as the pattern made visible. The reading is the sūrah's claim about the community's relation to its own history: the history is not a sequence of accidents, and the sequence is the pattern in its appearances. The sūrah's teaching of the reading is its way of saying that the community is not a spectator of its own history, and that the history is the community's school. The wont is the curriculum, and the event is the lesson, and the lesson is the sūrah's way of completing the education of the community that stands in the valley. The community that learns the reading is the community the sūrah addresses, and the address is the sūrah's way of completing its account of the event.

**The Verse That Connects the Two**

The position of the verse in the sūrah is the reason for its function. It stands between the counterfactual of the previous verse and the account of the holding back in the next, and the position is the work. The counterfactual is the first instance of the wont, the battle that would have come and would have ended in the flight, and the holding back is the second instance, the battle that did not come and ended in the treaty. The wont is the sūrah's way of saying that the two instances are the pattern, and that the pattern is the sūrah's claim about the event. The reader passes through the verse from one instance to the other, and the passing is the sūrah's way of stating that the event is the pattern, and the pattern is the sūrah's name for the dealings of God with the community that stands in his line.
verses.24:
> He is the One Who held back their hands from you and your hands from them in the valley of ˹Ḥudaibiyah, near˺ Mecca, after giving you the upper hand over ˹a group of˺ them. And Allah is All-Seeing of what you do

**The Double Holding Back**

The verse states the holding back in its full form, and the full form is the double act. He held back their hands from you, and your hands from them, and the doubling is the sūrah's way of saying that the peace was not the result of one side's restraint. The hands of the Quraysh were held back from the Muslims, and the hands of the Muslims were held back from the Quraysh, and the two holdings are the work of the one who holds both. The sūrah's statement of the double is its way of saying that the treaty was not a concession made by the weaker side to the stronger, and that the restraint was not the absence of the power to fight. The double holding is the sūrah's name for the peace, and the name is the sūrah's claim about the event.

**The Upper Hand That Was Given**

The verse states the holding back after the giving of the upper hand, and the sequence is the sūrah's way of fixing the ground of the restraint. After having made you victorious over them, the verse says, and the victory over them is the upper hand that the Muslims held before the hands were held back. The exegesis gives the reference of the upper hand in its account of the event, and the account is the group that attempted the surprise attack before the treaty was ratified. The Muslims had the upper hand over that group, and the upper hand is the sūrah's way of saying that the holding back was not the result of the Muslims' weakness. The restraint was made on the ground of the strength, and the ground is what the sūrah's sequence states. The verse's claim, by the sequence, is that the peace was the choice of the strong, and the choice is the sūrah's way of stating the event from the inside.

**Attackers Named in the Tradition**

The exegesis preserves the account that gives the upper hand its content, and the account is the sūrah's way of making the verse concrete. A group of young men, thirty on the more common count, attempted a surprise attack on the Muslims at Ḥudaibiyah before the treaty had been ratified, and the attempt was discovered. When the attackers were caught by the Muslims, the Prophet asked them whether they had come under the protection of someone, and when they said no, he let them go. Another account gives the number at eighty, and the account places the attack during the morning prayer. The two accounts are the range of the community's memory, and the range is the sūrah's way of keeping the event in its uncertainty. The sūrah's verse does not name the number or the hour, and the naming in the tradition is the community's way of making the verse's upper hand concrete. The upper hand was the fact of the capture, and the capture is what the letting go was the letting go of.

**The Letting Go as the Holding Back**

The letting go of the captured attackers is the sūrah's way of stating the holding back of the Muslims' hands in its active form. The Muslims had the attackers in their power, and the power was the upper hand, and the Prophet let them go, and the letting go is the holding back made into a choice. The peace at Ḥudaibiyah was not the absence of the fight, the sūrah's account implies; it was the choice of the peace on the ground of the ability to fight. The hands that were held back were the hands that could have struck, and the striking was the option that was refused, and the refusal is the sūrah's name for the restraint. The sūrah's statement of the event, in the verse and in the account it preserves, is its way of saying that the peace was an act, not an accident, and that the act was the act of the one who held the upper hand.

**The Seeing That Closes the Account**

The verse closes with the name of the Seeing, and the closing is the sūrah's way of stating that the event is seen. Allah is All-Seeing of what you do, and the seeing is the sūrah's way of saying that the holding back is seen, and that the letting go is seen, and that the choice of the peace is seen. The sūrah's closing of the account of the event with the Seeing is its way of saying that the event is not a private matter of the community. The community's choice in the valley outside Mecca, the choice that held back its hands and let go its captives, is the choice that stands before the one who sees, and the standing is the sūrah's way of completing the account. The sūrah's second half has now stated the reward, the counterfactual, the wont, and the holding back, and the Seeing is the sūrah's way of saying that all of it is seen. The sūrah's remaining verses will state the event's meaning in its full form, and the seeing is the ground on which that meaning stands, the ground the sūrah has now laid for its final movement.
